background.definition: AV block is defined as an abnormal delay or interruption in the conduction of atrial impulses to ventricles due to anatomic lesions or increase in the refractory period of the conduction pathway.

list.listitem: Incidence increases with age.
The Framingham study found interventricular block in 6% of males and 2.4% of females, with only half of the blocks in both sexes being complete.
Idiopathic fibrosis and sclerosis.
Ischemic heart disease, especially inferior, septal, and right ventricle.
Drugs like beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin, and amiodarone.
Increased vagal tone, including in well-trained athletes.
Valvulopathy such as calcification of the aortic and mitral valve.

Other causes including cardiomyopathies, collagen vascular diseases, amyloidosis, hemochromatosis, myocarditis, infiltrative malignancies, sarcoidosis, trauma from valve surgeries, endocarditis, Lyme disease, and sleep apnea.
Congenital block.
Electrolyte imbalances such as hyperkalemia.

AV block can result from conduction block in the atrium, AV node, and His-Purkinje system. Damage to conduction fibers in any part from the above mentioned causes can lead to disturbance in the conduction of impulses from atria to ventricle. Severity of block ranges from first degree to third degree.
First-degree AV block usually results from conduction delay within the AV node and rarely from intra-atrial or His-Purkinje causes.

Mobitz type I, second-degree block with normal QRS interval, is almost always in the AV node and due to decremental conduction. Mobitz type I, second-degree block with prolonged QRS interval may be in the AV node, His-Purkinje system, or both.

Mobitz type II, second-degree block, frequently progresses to complete AV block. Mobitz type II AV block usually occurs in the presence of bundle branch block and is almost always in the His-Purkinje system.
A 2:1 AV block (advanced second degree) with normal QRS duration or with a normal P-R interval suggests block in the AV node, but a wide QRS suggests the presence of infranodal block.
Patients with type II or type I block, when associated with bundle branch block, are at high risk for development of higher degrees of AV block.
Complete or third-degree AV block may occur at AV node (narrow QRS) or at the His-Purkinje system (wide QRS). The more distal the block, the slower the escape rhythm.
Routine 12-lead ECG is usually adequate to establish the degree and site of AV block. C
Consider electrophysiologic study for patients in whom the cause of syncope has not been established and a high-degree AV block is suspected. C

list.listitem: First-degree block: PR interval greater than 200 msec.

Second-degree block (Mobitz I): progressive PR prolongation and shortening of RR interval until P wave is blocked. Pause after blocked P wave is less than twice the PP interval. PR following block is shorter than PR immediately preceding block.
Second-degree block (Mobitz II): regular sinus/atrial rhythm with intermittent nonconducted P waves. Constant PR interval in the conducted beats.

Advanced or high-degree AV block: second-degree AV block often characterized by multiple, successive nonconducted P waves and otherwise not consistent with Mobitz I or II that is ongoing or frequently reccuring. Atrial activation followed by ventricular activation occuring at a 2:1 ratio can be categorized in this manner. Wide QRS complex in the setting of 2:1 block suggests high grade block at the level of the His bundle or below.

Third-degree AV block (complete heart block): characterized by independent atrial and ventricular complexes with atrial rate usually exceeding ventricular rate (American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Task Force Definitions for Electrophysiological Studies, 2006).

First-degree AV block is usually asymptomatic, but marked block with PR greater than 300 msec can lead to symptoms similar to pacemaker syndrome due to loss of AV synchrony. In patients with underlying left ventricular (LV) dysfunction, it may result in worsening heart failure.

S1 is decreased in intensity, short diastolic murmur may be heard at the cardiac apex, long "a–c" interval (interval between atrial contraction and ventricular isovolumic systole) is found on jugular venous pulse, and rarely giant "a" waves are seen when PR is markedly prolonged.

Mobitz type I AV block is usually asymptomatic, but a few patients may complain of symptoms of low cardiac output (angina or syncope) from slow sinus rate (2:1 or 3:2 block). Mobitz I usually occurs in normal individuals with high vagal tone, athletes, elderly, those on AV blocking medications, and those with myocarditis and inferoposterior infarction from right coronary artery (90%) or left circumflex (10%) obstruction.

Mobitz type II block is permanent, carries a bad prognosis, and frequently progresses to third-degree block. Increase in the heart rate with exercise can worsen the AV block and can lead to exercise intolerance, dizziness, presyncope, or syncope (Stokes-Adams attacks).
The "a wave" is not followed by the "v wave" whenever a beat is dropped. In Mobitz type I, S1 is diminished, and the a-c interval widens with each PR prolongation similar to first-degree block.

Third-degree block is accompanied by slower escape pacemaker resulting in symptoms of reduced cardiac output from bradycardia. Patients often complain of fatigue, dizziness, angina, dyspnea, presyncope or syncope (Stokes-Adams attacks), and palpitations. They are at high risk for sudden cardiac death.
Bradycardia with variable intensity of S1, cannon a waves, and signs of congestive heart failure (CHF) may be present.

Routine 12-lead ECG is usually adequate to establish the varying degree and site of AV block. PR interval, relationship of P wave to QRS complex, QRS duration, and the presence of an escape rhythm can provide clues to the degree of block.
Atropine, vagal maneuvers, and exercise are sometime helpful in further establishing the level of block.

In patients with paroxysmal symptoms, consider 24- to 48-hour Holter monitoring, 30-day event monitoring, or outpatient continous telemetry monitoring using newer technology like patch technology or ECG app on smartphone 1-year implantable loop recording if no abnormalities are seen on ECG. Notably, evidence is lacking with regard to how smartphone based monitoring impacts patient outcomes.
Consider electrophysiologic study when the cause of syncope has not been established and if high-grade AV block is suspected.
Echocardiogram can be done to rule out any structural heart disease, valvulopathy and endocarditis.

Drug therapy is reserved for treatment of high grade AV block in the emergency setting until cardiac pacing can be initiated. C
Permanent pacing is recommended for symptomatic patients with Mobitz II second- and third-degree AV block. B
Permanent pacing is recommended in third-degree and advanced second-degree patients with documented asystole of 3 seconds or greater or escape rate less than 40 beats/min. C
Drug therapy is reserved for treatment of high grade AV block in the emergency setting until cardiac pacing can be initiated.
Intravenous atropine, isoproterenol, and dopamine can be used acutely in patients with symptomatic bradycardia. Chronic use is not recommended due to significant side effects.
Atropine is not recommended in patients with infranodal block as it can decrease ventricular rate further.
Isoproterenol and dopamine are not recommended to treat bradyarrhythmias resulting from myocardial ischemia secondary to their arrhythmogenicity.
See .
Patients with persistent and symptomatic second- or third-degree AV block resulting from acute myocardial ischemia are also candidates for permanent pacing.

Dual-chamber pacing is more effective than single-chamber ventricular pacing with regard to pacemaker syndrome and exercise capacity but without any significant other favorable outcomes (although a pooled analysis shows a non-significant trend in favor of fewer strokes, less heart failure, and lower mortality with dual chamber pacing).
"Leadless" pacer systems are currently underdevelopment and are being evaluated in clinical trials.
In acute emergency, temporary pacing via a transcutaneous or transvenous route should be done until AV block resolves or as a bridge to a permanent cardiac pacemaker.
Stop calcium channel blockers, beta blockers, and digoxin.
Consider using IV glucagon in beta blocker or calcium channel blocker overdose.
Correct electrolyte abnormalities.
Treat infectious causes such as endocarditis or Lyme carditis.
Hospitalize patients with symptomatic AV block to confirm the diagnosis.
Also hospitalize to address reversible causes such as myocardial ischemia and to determine the need for electrophysiologic studies and pacemaker placement.
Stokes-Adams syndrome: pacemaker implantation.
Heart failure: pacemaker implantation.
Permanent pacing improves survival in third-degree and advanced second-degree AV block. B
Even patients with first-degree AV block are at higher risk for later atrial fibrillation and pacemaker implantation. B
Schedule follow-up for patients with AV block depending on the type of pacemaker implanted and their management needs. C
Prognosis of patients with first-degree and second-degree Mobitz type I is good even without treatment.

First-degree heart block with moderate PR prolongation (0.22-0.23 second) was traditionally thought to be a benign condition. However, a recent study using Framingham data looked at outcomes for 124 individuals (mean age 49 years) with a PR interval greater than 200 msec at baseline in 1968-1974 who were followed through 2007. The risk of atrial fibrillation (NNH 96), pacemaker implantation (NNH 189) and all-cause mortality (NNH 49) was greater in patients with first degree block than those without.

In a study of 3416 patients age 60 years or older presenting with syncope or near-syncope to the ED but without serious cardiac arrhythmia identified at the time of the visit, first degree AV block was one of the predictors of a serious arrhythmia being diagnosed in the next month. Other ECG predictors included non-sinus rhythm, short PR interval, complete LBBB, and indicators of acute or chronic ischemia.

Patients with high-grade AV block or complete AV block are at increased risk of CHF and Stokes-Adams syndrome. One-year survival of patients not paced after Stokes-Adams syndrome is 50%. Occasionally long survival is possible despite Stokes-Adams syndrome.
The prognosis of second-degree Mobitz type II and complete heart block after pacemaker implantation is good.
Survival of paced individuals is 80% in 1 year and 60% at 5 years.
Pacemaker implantation regardless of the pacing mode is associated with improvements in quality of life.
Close follow-up is needed for Mobitz type II second-degree block patients, as it frequently progresses to complete block.
Assess pacemaker function before discharge after pacemaker implantation.
Periodic transtelephonic monitoring with intermittent clinic evaluation is needed to assess pacemaker function.

Clinic follow-up includes assessment of the clinical status of the patient, battery status, pacing threshold, pulse width, sensing function, lead integrity, and optimization of sensor-driven rate response.
Avoid AV blocking medications.
Avoid strong magnetic fields if pacemaker is implanted.
In case of any symptoms, patient should follow up with clinic immediately.
A complete heart block rarely causes any problems during pregnancy.
Symptomatic patients in the first and second term are candidates for permanent pacemaker.
Symptomatic patients who present at term may require temporary pacing with induction of delivery.

Valsalva maneuver during labor can further slow down the heart in pregnant patients with complete heart block, resulting in syncope and convulsions. All women with complete heart block should have either temporary or permanent pacemeker support during labor.

Permanent pacing is recommended in children with advanced second- or third-degree AV block associated with symptomatic bradycardia. Dilated cardiomyopathy is a possible complication following pacemaker implantation in this group.
Congenital third-degree AV block is possible with wide QRS escape rhythm.
Congenital third-degree AV block is possible in the infant with a ventricular rate of less than 50 beats/min.
